title: A world of dew
hookLine: after his daughter's death, Issa: this world of dew is a world of dew, and yet (1819)
tomorrow: why would a grieving poet beg you not to swat a fly?

cards: When someone loses a person they love, the comments fill up with the same kind lines: everything happens for a reason, nothing lasts, let it go.
In a mountain village in Japan, the poet Issa sits beside his little daughter, Sato. She has smallpox. In his journal of that year he writes it down: the fever, the hope, the turn for the worse.
Then she is gone. And the comfort people offer him is an old Buddhist one: this life is only dew.

teach.b: Dew is a Buddhist picture. The Diamond Sutra closes by saying that everything made is like a dream, a bubble, a shadow, like dew or a flash of lightning.
That's impermanence, the Buddha's teaching that nothing put together stays. Issa knew it well; he was a devout follower of Pure Land Buddhism.
And he answered with this poem, in Japanese: tsuyu no yo wa, tsuyu no yo nagara, sari nagara. This world of dew is a world of dew, and yet, and yet. Look at how it's built.
The first two lines agree with the teaching completely. Yes. It's dew.
Then two small words, sari nagara: and yet. He doesn't argue with the Buddha, and he doesn't pretend it doesn't hurt.
Notice the first half says the same word twice, dew and dew, as if he's turning the teaching over in his hands.
Some readers hear Issa's own Pure Land path in what comes next.
Pure Land leans on the compassion of Amida Buddha rather than on one's own calm, so in that reading a grieving father doesn't have to be serene first to be held.
Something to tell a friend tonight: his pen name, Issa, is written with the characters for one and tea.

how: Readers of haiku may read Issa's dew poem slowly, sometimes aloud, beside their own losses. In Japanese Buddhism, teaching about impermanence sits alongside funeral and memorial rites that let families grieve.

games.q: what does “a world of dew” mean?
o: a poem about waking early to watch the sunrise
a Buddhist picture of life, brief as morning dew
a farmer's name for the wet weeks before harvest

games.q: the poem and its teaching: tap the pairs.
p: the poet who lost his daughter Sato
a Buddhist picture of what passes
likens made things to dew and lightning

s: Issa's pen name is written with the characters for 'one' and 'tea'
一茶: issa, one and tea.
the picture of life as dew comes from Buddhist teaching
the Diamond Sutra closes by likening everything made to dew, a dream, a bubble.
Issa's poem argues that the Buddha was wrong
two lines agree: the world is dew. the 'and yet' adds grief; it doesn't take the truth back.

games.q: at a memorial, a relative tells the widow, "it's all impermanent, so don't be sad." what would Issa's poem say back?
o: it's all dew, and yet: both are true, and grief belongs here.
the relative is right; a real Buddhist wouldn't grieve.
impermanence is too sad an idea to say at a memorial.
games.why: Issa agrees with the teaching in two lines, then writes 'and yet.' he keeps impermanence and keeps the grief.

practice: Name, quietly, one thing in your life that's passing: a season, a place, someone getting older. Say the true part first, under your breath: this is passing. Then add the two words Issa added: and yet.
Let the quiet hold both halves without choosing one.

wordCard.voice: A world of dew: the Buddhist picture of a life that passes, and the opening of Issa's poem for his daughter.

orig.s: 露の世は露の世ながらさりながら
orig.say: tsoo-YOO no yo wa, tsoo-YOO no yo nah-GAH-rah, SAH-ree nah-GAH-rah
orig.note: Japanese: this world of dew is a world of dew, and yet, and yet. Issa's poem for his daughter.

carryVoice: Your line: and yet. The dew is real, and so is the grief. Say it once today, when something ends.

sources.ref: Issa, haiku on the death of his daughter Sato, in Oraga Haru (The Year of My Life)
